title: Ancient Greece
bigQuestion: How did a small, rocky land of quarreling city-states produce ideas that still shape how we govern, think and speak?

story.title: The Rope and the Hill
story.kicker: On a morning in Athens around 430 BCE, a potter drops his work and hurries uphill, because today the city will decide about war.
paragraphs: The sun is barely over the hills when Demos, a potter, wipes the clay from his hands and leaves his shop. He is not in trouble and he is not late for work. He is going to vote. Today the Assembly of Athens meets on the Pnyx, a bare rock hill west of the Acropolis. Any male citizen over eighteen may come, speak and raise his hand. Demos has never been rich, but here his hand counts the same as a nobleman's.

In the marketplace, city slaves stretch a long rope dipped in red paint and sweep it across the crowd. Any man caught with red on his cloak was dawdling instead of going to the Assembly, and he can be fined. Demos hurries ahead of the rope. He climbs the stone steps with farmers, sailors, shopkeepers and a few wealthy men in fine wool. Perhaps six thousand people crowd onto the slope, facing a carved stone platform where speakers stand.

A herald calls out, "Who wishes to speak?" One man argues that Athens should send ships to help an ally. Another warns that the treasury is low and the enemy is strong. Demos listens and thinks about his brother, who rows in the fleet. No one asked Demos to be an expert. The Athenians believed that ordinary people, hearing both sides, could judge well enough.

Not everyone is on the hill. Demos's wife, Melitta, is at home; women cannot vote. His neighbor Nikias, a skilled metalworker born in another city, pays taxes but has no vote either. The enslaved man who grinds Demos's clay has no say at all. Athenian democracy was real, and it was also narrow. Out of perhaps three hundred thousand people in Athens and the land around it, only about thirty to forty thousand were voting citizens.

When the speeches end, the herald calls for a show of hands. Officials count roughly by eye. Demos raises his hand with the majority, and the matter is settled. He walks back down to his shop knowing that he, a potter, helped decide the policy of a great city. Two and a half thousand years later, that idea still seems remarkable.
story.think: Athens let a potter vote on war but not his wife or his foreign-born neighbor. Was Athens a democracy? What would you need to know to decide?

lessons.title: Mountains, Sea and the Polis
lessons.mainIdea: Greece's mountains and coast split its people into small, independent city-states that shared a language and gods.
reading: Look at a map of Greece and you see a ragged land. Mountains cover most of it. The coast twists into bays and peninsulas, and hundreds of islands dot the Aegean Sea. Farmland lies in small valleys cut off from each other by rock. The soil is thin and dry. Wheat grows poorly, but olives and grapes do well on the hillsides, and the sea is never far away.

This geography shaped Greek life. A valley could not easily rule the next valley over the mountains, so each one became its own tiny country. The Greeks called such a community a *polis*, which we translate as city-state. A polis was a town, the farmland around it and the people who belonged to it. There were hundreds of them, most with only a few thousand people. Each had its own laws, army and coins.

Because farming was hard, Greeks became sailors and traders. They sailed to Egypt for grain and to Italy for metals. By about 600 BCE they had planted *colonies*, new city-states, around the Black Sea and along the coasts of Italy, France and North Africa. A colony kept the mother city's gods and customs but ruled itself.

The city-states fought each other often, yet they knew they were all Greek. They spoke the same language, worshiped the same gods and gathered every four years at Olympia for athletic games in honor of Zeus. Wars stopped for the games. A Greek from Sparta and a Greek from Athens might be enemies, but both called outsiders *barbarians*, people whose speech sounded like "bar-bar" to them.

words.d: a Greek city-state: a town, its farmland and its citizens, ruling itself
a new settlement founded far away by a city-state, keeping its customs
the Greek word for anyone who did not speak Greek

look.title: Two Valleys
look.text: Imagine two farming villages ten miles apart, with a rocky mountain between them. Walking over takes a full day. Each village has its own spring, fields and temple. When a stranger arrives, each village has to decide alone whether to let him stay.
look.prompt: Why might these two villages end up with different laws and leaders, even though they speak the same language?

check.q: What was a polis?
choices: A self-governing city-state with its own laws
A Greek temple on a hill
A large empire ruled by a king
A ship used for trading grain
check.why: A polis was a city, its farmland and its citizens, governing itself. Greece had hundreds of them.

check.q: Why did Greece split into many small city-states instead of one country?
choices: The Greeks did not share a language
Mountains and the sea cut communities off from each other
A king ordered the land divided
check.why: Mountains made it hard for one valley to rule another, so each community governed itself.

check.q: What did all Greeks share, even when their city-states were at war?
check.why: City-states had their own laws and coins, but all Greeks spoke Greek, worshiped the same gods and met at Olympia.

lessons.title: Athens and Sparta
lessons.mainIdea: Athens and Sparta were both Greek, but one built a trading democracy and the other a military state.
reading: The two most powerful city-states could hardly have been more different. *Athens* sat near the sea in the region of Attica. It grew rich from trade, silver mines and the olive oil it shipped abroad. Athenians prized speaking well, building beautifully and arguing about ideas. By the fifth century BCE, its citizens governed themselves in an assembly.

*Sparta* lay inland in a valley of the Peloponnese, the southern peninsula. Long before, the Spartans had conquered their neighbors and turned them into *helots*, farm workers who belonged to the state. Helots outnumbered Spartans many times over. To keep them down, Sparta became an army. Two kings led it in war, and a council of elders and a small assembly ran the city.

A Spartan boy left his family at age seven to live in barracks. He learned to endure cold, hunger and beatings. Every Spartan man was a full-time soldier until age sixty, and the helots did the farming. Spartan women had more freedom than Athenian women. They ran the households, owned land and trained in sports so they would have strong children. Spartans distrusted trade, coins and new ideas.

Athenians thought Spartans were grim and closed-minded. Spartans thought Athenians were soft and talked too much. Yet the Greek world respected Sparta's soldiers and Athens's ships. When a great danger came from the east, the two rivals would have to fight side by side.

words.d: a sea-trading city-state in Attica known for democracy, art and philosophy
an inland city-state in the Peloponnese organized around its army
a conquered person forced to farm for Sparta

look.title: Two Boys at Seven
look.text: One boy in Athens goes to a teacher each morning to learn reading, music and wrestling, then helps in his father's shop. One boy in Sparta moves into a barracks with other boys, gets one cloak a year and is punished if he is caught stealing food, though not for stealing it.
look.prompt: What did each city want its boys to become? What does that tell you about what each city feared?

check.q: Why did Sparta organize its whole society around the army?
choices: To control the helots, who greatly outnumbered Spartans
check.why: The helots were conquered farm workers who far outnumbered Spartans. Sparta stayed armed to keep them down.

check.q: Which of these was true of Athens but not Sparta?
choices: It grew wealthy from sea trade and silver
Boys left home at seven for barracks
Women owned land and trained in sports
check.why: Athens was a sea-trading city rich from silver and olive oil. The other choices describe Sparta.

check.q: Compared with Athenian women, Spartan women had:
choices: The same rights, including the vote
The duty to serve as soldiers
check.why: Spartan women ran households, owned land and trained in sports, which Athenian women could not do.

lessons.title: How Athens Became a Democracy
lessons.mainIdea: Over about two centuries, reformers gave ordinary Athenian citizens the power to make laws and judge cases.
reading: Athens was not always a democracy. Around 600 BCE, nobles ran the city and poor farmers who fell into debt could be sold as slaves. Anger grew. In 594 BCE the Athenians chose a respected leader named *Solon* to fix things. He canceled the debts, freed those enslaved for debt and let all citizens, not just nobles, sit in the assembly and serve on juries. Nobles still held most offices.

Later, a strongman named Peisistratus seized power as a *tyrant*. To the Greeks that word meant a ruler who took power by force, not always a cruel one. His sons ruled after him until they were driven out. Then, in 508 BCE, a noble named *Cleisthenes* rebuilt the government. He broke up the old family power blocs and mixed citizens from different regions into ten new tribes. Each tribe sent fifty men, chosen by lottery, to a Council of Five Hundred that prepared business for the assembly.

The Athenians called their system *democracy*, from demos, the people, and kratos, power. Its heart was the Assembly, where every citizen could speak and vote directly. Most officials were picked by drawing lots, on the idea that any citizen was fit to serve for a year. Only generals were elected, since war needed skill. Large juries of hundreds of citizens decided court cases with no judge to overrule them.

The Athenians even had a way to protect democracy from an ambitious man. Once a year the Assembly could vote to banish someone for ten years. Citizens scratched a name on a piece of broken pottery called an ostrakon. If enough named the same person, he had to leave. Our word ostracize comes from this. Archaeologists have dug up thousands of these pottery votes with real names on them.

words.d: Athenian leader who canceled debts and opened the assembly to all citizens around 594 BCE
in Greek, a ruler who seized power by force rather than by law
Athenian reformer of 508 BCE who built the system of tribes and the Council of Five Hundred
rule by the people; in Athens, citizens voting directly in an assembly

look.title: Building Athenian Democracy
look.cite: standard dates and figures for classical Athens
look.prompt: About how many years passed between Solon's reforms and Cleisthenes' reforms? Why might big changes in government take that long?

check.q: What did Solon do for poor Athenians around 594 BCE?
choices: Gave them free land in colonies
Canceled their debts and freed those enslaved for debt
check.why: Solon's reforms ended debt slavery and let all citizens join the assembly and juries.

check.q: How were most Athenian officials chosen?
choices: By election of the whole city
check.why: Most offices went by lottery, on the idea that any citizen could serve. Only generals were elected.

check.q: What was the purpose of the pottery votes called ostraka?
choices: To banish a man who seemed too powerful
To elect the Council of Five Hundred
check.why: Once a year citizens could vote to send someone into exile for ten years, protecting democracy from a would-be tyrant.

lessons.title: Who Was Left Out
lessons.mainIdea: Athenian democracy included every male citizen but shut out women, foreigners and the enslaved, who together were most of the population.
reading: Athenian democracy was direct: citizens did not send representatives, they showed up and voted. But who counted as a citizen? By the middle of the fifth century BCE, a man had to be born to an Athenian father and an Athenian mother, be free and be at least eighteen. Scholars estimate the citizens numbered roughly thirty to forty thousand adult men, out of a total population in Attica of perhaps three hundred thousand.

Women of citizen families were expected to stay mostly at home, weave cloth and manage the household. They could not vote, hold office or own much property in their own name. A woman's father or husband spoke for her in court. Poorer women did work outside, selling in the market or farming, but still had no political voice.

*Metics* were free people from other places who lived in Athens. Many were skilled craftsmen, merchants and bankers. They paid a special tax and served in the army, but they could not vote or own land. The philosopher Aristotle himself lived in Athens as a metic. Below them were the enslaved. Perhaps one in three people in Athens was enslaved. They worked in homes, workshops, farms and, worst of all, the silver mines. Athens's wealth rested on their labor.

So the same city that invented rule by the people also ruled over most of its people without their consent. Historians point this out not to dismiss Athens but to be accurate. The Athenians opened a door that had never been opened. They also decided, deliberately, how narrow the doorway would be. Every democracy since has had to answer the same question: who counts?

words.d: in Athens, a free adult man born to Athenian parents, with the right to vote
a free foreigner living in Athens who paid taxes but could not vote or own land

look.title: Who Lived in Athens, about 430 BCE
look.cite: modern scholarly estimates, heavily rounded; exact figures are unknown
look.prompt: About what share of the people in Athens could vote? What would change if you counted only adults?

check.q: Which group could vote in the Athenian Assembly?
choices: Free adult men born to Athenian parents
All free adults, men and women
Anyone who served in the army
check.why: Only free adult men with Athenian parents were citizens. Metics served in the army and paid taxes but could not vote.

check.q: Roughly what share of the population of Athens was enslaved?
check.why: Scholars estimate that perhaps a third of the people in Athens were enslaved, working in homes, farms and mines.

check.q: Why do historians stress who was excluded from Athenian democracy?
choices: To show that Sparta was fairer
Because Athens had no real laws
To describe Athens accurately, both its new idea and its limits
check.why: The lesson says historians point this out to be accurate, not to dismiss Athens.

lessons.title: The Persian Wars
lessons.mainIdea: Outnumbered Greek city-states twice turned back the huge Persian Empire, at Marathon and then at Salamis and Plataea.
reading: To the east of Greece lay the largest empire the world had yet seen. The *Persian Empire* stretched from Egypt to the edge of India. Its king, Darius, ruled millions of people. When Greek cities on the coast of Asia Minor rebelled against him, Athens sent ships to help. Darius crushed the revolt and decided to punish Athens.

In 490 BCE a Persian army landed at the plain of *Marathon*, about twenty-six miles from Athens. The Athenians, with help from one small ally, marched out to meet them. The Greeks fought as *hoplites*, heavily armored foot soldiers who locked shields in a tight block called a phalanx. They charged at a run and broke the Persian line. The story that a runner raced to Athens with news of victory gave the marathon race its name and distance.

Ten years later Darius's son Xerxes came back with a far larger force by land and sea. At the narrow pass of Thermopylae, a small Greek army led by three hundred Spartans held the road for days until they were surrounded and killed. The Persians burned Athens. But the Athenian leader Themistocles had persuaded his city to build a navy with its silver. In 480 BCE, in the narrow strait of *Salamis*, the Greek ships rammed and sank the crowded Persian fleet while Xerxes watched from shore.

The next year a united Greek army defeated the Persians at Plataea, and the invasion was over. How do we know all this? Mostly from one man, the historian Herodotus, who traveled, asked questions and wrote it down a few decades later. The victory left Athens with the strongest navy in Greece and a new confidence. Its greatest age was about to begin.

words.d: the vast empire east of Greece, stretching from Egypt to India
plain near Athens where the Athenians defeated a Persian army in 490 BCE
a Greek foot soldier with heavy armor and a large shield who fought in a phalanx
the strait where the Greek navy destroyed the Persian fleet in 480 BCE

look.title: Herodotus Explains His Purpose
look.text: Herodotus of Halicarnassus set down his inquiry, he wrote, so that the deeds of people would not fade with time, so that the great achievements of both Greeks and barbarians would not go unremembered, and to show why they went to war with each other.
look.cite: Herodotus, opening of the Histories, about 430 BCE (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Herodotus promised to record the deeds of Persians as well as Greeks. Why does that matter for whether we can trust him?

check.q: What was a phalanx?
choices: A tight block of armored soldiers with locked shields
check.why: Hoplites fought in a phalanx, a close formation of shields and spears that broke the Persian line at Marathon.

check.q: Why was building a navy so important for Athens before 480 BCE?
choices: It let the Greeks destroy the Persian fleet at Salamis
Ships were needed to escape to Egypt
The Persians had no ships of their own
check.why: Themistocles used silver to build ships, and that fleet won the decisive battle in the strait of Salamis.

check.q: Where does most of our knowledge of the Persian Wars come from?
choices: The historian Herodotus, who asked questions and wrote it down
check.why: Herodotus traveled, interviewed people and wrote his Histories a few decades after the wars.

lessons.title: The Parthenon and the Theater
lessons.mainIdea: In the fifty years after the Persian Wars, Athens used its wealth to build the Parthenon and to invent drama.
reading: After the Persians left, Athens led a league of Greek cities that paid money into a common fund for defense. Under the leader *Pericles*, Athens moved that treasury to its own city and spent much of it at home. Many allies were angry. Athens was becoming an empire. But the money built something the world still visits.

On the *Acropolis*, the rocky hill above the city, the Athenians raised a marble temple to their goddess Athena. The *Parthenon* took about fifteen years to build, from 447 to 432 BCE. Its columns lean slightly inward and its floor curves slightly upward, tricks that make it look perfectly straight to the eye. Inside stood a statue of Athena forty feet tall, covered in gold and ivory. Sculptors carved a band of figures around the building showing the people of Athens in procession.

Down the hill, in an open-air theater cut into the slope, Athenians invented *drama*. Plays began as songs to the god Dionysus and grew into stories acted by masked performers with a singing chorus. Tragedies by Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides showed kings and heroes destroyed by pride or fate. Comedies by Aristophanes made fun of politicians, philosophers and the war, sometimes with the targets sitting in the audience.

Theater was not a small hobby. Thousands of citizens attended festivals that lasted days, and the city paid for poor citizens' tickets. Watching a play meant thinking together about justice, power and grief. Many of these plays survive, and theaters still perform them. Our words theater, drama, tragedy, comedy and chorus are all Greek.

words.d: leader of Athens in its golden age, about 460 to 429 BCE
the high rock in Athens where the main temples stood
the marble temple to Athena built on the Acropolis from 447 to 432 BCE
plays acted out for an audience; Athenians invented tragedy and comedy

look.title: Pericles Praises Athens
look.text: In a speech honoring the war dead, Pericles said that Athens's government was called a democracy because it served the many, not the few. In private disputes everyone was equal before the law, he said, and a man was chosen for public office by his ability, not his class. Poverty was no bar if a man could serve the city.
look.cite: Pericles' funeral speech, as recorded by the historian Thucydides, about 431 BCE (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Pericles was speaking at a funeral in wartime. How might that setting shape what he chose to say about Athens?

check.q: Where did much of the money to build the Parthenon come from?
choices: A defense fund paid by Athens's allies
check.why: Pericles moved the league treasury to Athens and spent much of it on the city, which angered the allies.

check.q: Why do the Parthenon's columns lean slightly inward?
choices: So the building looks perfectly straight to the eye
Because the builders made a mistake
To hold up the gold statue
So the roof could drain rain
check.why: The builders used small curves and leans to correct how the eye sees, making the temple look straight.

check.q: What did Aristophanes do that shows how free Athenian theater was?
choices: He made fun of living politicians who might be in the audience
He refused to use a chorus
check.why: His comedies mocked real leaders and thinkers, sometimes while they watched.

lessons.title: Socrates, Plato and Aristotle
lessons.mainIdea: Three Athenian thinkers taught people to question, reason and observe, and their methods are still used today.
reading: *Philosophy* means love of wisdom. Greek philosophers tried to understand the world by reasoning rather than by retelling myths. The most famous of them, *Socrates*, wrote nothing at all. He walked the streets of Athens in the late fifth century BCE asking people what they meant by words like courage, justice and goodness. When they answered, he asked another question, and another, until they saw that they did not really know. Teachers still call this the Socratic method.

Many Athenians found him annoying, and some found him dangerous. In 399 BCE, after Athens had lost a long war with Sparta, a jury of citizens convicted Socrates of not respecting the city's gods and corrupting the young. He refused to beg or to flee. He drank the poison hemlock as the law required. His death showed both the freedom of Athens, which had let him question everything for decades, and its limits.

His student *Plato* wrote down conversations, called dialogues, in which Socrates is the main speaker. Plato founded a school in Athens called the Academy. He argued that the things we see are imperfect copies of perfect ideas, and that the best state would be run by wise rulers, not by the crowd that had killed his teacher. Plato did not trust democracy.

Plato's student *Aristotle* took a different path. He wanted to look at the actual world. He collected and described animals, studied the constitutions of more than a hundred Greek cities, wrote the first books on logic and gave rules for good plays. Aristotle's habit of careful observation and sorting things into categories became a model for science. For a while he was also tutor to a prince in Macedon named Alexander.

words.d: the search for wisdom through reasoning about big questions
Athenian thinker who taught by asking questions; executed in 399 BCE
student of Socrates who wrote dialogues and founded the Academy
student of Plato who studied nature and logic by careful observation

look.title: The Questioner
look.text: A general tells Socrates that courage is standing firm in battle. Socrates asks: what about a soldier who wisely retreats to fight later? The general agrees that can be brave too. So courage is not just standing firm. Then what is it? The general has led armies, but now he is not sure.
look.prompt: Why might people find this kind of questioning both useful and irritating? When is it worth doing?

check.q: What was the Socratic method?
choices: Asking question after question to test what people think they know
Voting on the truth in the Assembly
check.why: Socrates taught by questioning until people saw the gaps in their own ideas.

check.q: What happened to Socrates in 399 BCE?
choices: An Athenian jury sentenced him to death
check.why: A citizen jury convicted him of disrespecting the gods and corrupting the young, and he drank hemlock.

check.q: How did Aristotle's approach differ from Plato's?
choices: He observed and classified the real world rather than seeking perfect ideas
check.why: Aristotle studied animals, constitutions and logic by observation, while Plato reasoned about perfect ideas.

lessons.title: History and Medicine
lessons.mainIdea: Greek writers began to explain wars and diseases by evidence and natural causes instead of by the will of the gods.
reading: Before the Greeks, people recorded kings' victories, but no one had asked, in a careful way, why events happened. *Herodotus*, born in the 480s BCE, did. He traveled through Egypt, Persia and Greece, listened to priests, soldiers and merchants, and compared their stories. Sometimes he reported tales he doubted and said so. Later writers named him the father of history, and the word history comes from his Greek word for inquiry.

Thucydides, an Athenian general, went further. He wrote the story of the long war between Athens and Sparta, from 431 to 404 BCE, which he had lived through. He left out the gods, checked witnesses against each other and looked for causes in fear, ambition and self-interest. He said he wrote not to entertain but to be useful to anyone who wanted to understand how people behave.

Doctors were making the same turn. On the island of Kos, a physician named *Hippocrates* and his followers taught that disease had natural causes, such as diet, climate and the body's balance, not angry gods. They watched patients closely and wrote down what they saw, day by day. A famous Hippocratic text on epilepsy, then called the sacred disease, argued that it was no more sacred than any other illness.

The Hippocratic writers were often wrong about the body. They had not dissected humans and believed health depended on four fluids they called humors. But their method, observe, record, look for natural causes, was the right one. Doctors today still speak of the Hippocratic Oath, a promise to help patients and do no harm, which grew from that school.

words.d: Greek writer of the 400s BCE called the father of history for his inquiry into the Persian Wars
Greek physician whose school taught that disease has natural causes
facts, records and observations used to support a claim

look.title: Thucydides on His Method
look.text: Thucydides wrote that he did not simply accept the first account he heard, or trust his own impressions. He checked each event as carefully as he could, either from his own experience or from witnesses, whose reports he tested, because different witnesses gave different accounts depending on their memory or their side.
look.cite: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, late 400s BCE (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Thucydides says witnesses disagree because of memory or their side. Give an example from your own life where that happens.

check.q: What does the word history originally mean in Greek?
check.why: Herodotus called his work an inquiry, and our word history comes from it.

check.q: How did Thucydides try to make his history reliable?
choices: He asked the gods through oracles
He wrote only what Athens's leaders said
He compared witnesses and left out the gods
check.why: Thucydides checked witnesses against each other and looked for human causes like fear and ambition.

check.q: What was the main new idea of the Hippocratic doctors?
choices: Disease has natural causes that can be observed
The four humors were always correct
Dissecting bodies is the key to medicine
check.why: They rejected angry gods as the cause of disease and watched patients closely, even though they were wrong about the humors.

lessons.title: Alexander the Great
lessons.mainIdea: In just over a decade, Alexander of Macedon conquered the Persian Empire and spread Greek culture from Egypt to India.
reading: The long war between Athens and Sparta left the Greek city-states weak. To their north lay *Macedon*, a kingdom the Greeks considered half-barbarian. Its king, Philip II, built a professional army with long pikes and clever tactics. In 338 BCE he defeated the Greek cities and forced them into a league under his control. Two years later he was murdered, and his son Alexander became king at age twenty.

*Alexander* had been tutored by Aristotle and had grown up on the poems of Homer. In 334 BCE he led about forty thousand men across into Asia to attack the Persian Empire. He won battle after battle, at the river Granicus, at Issus and at Gaugamela in 331 BCE, where he broke the army of King Darius III. He took Egypt, where he was welcomed as pharaoh, and the great cities of Babylon and Persepolis.

He kept marching east, through what is now Afghanistan and into the Indus valley of India. His soldiers, exhausted after eight years of fighting, finally refused to go farther. Alexander turned back. In 323 BCE, in Babylon, he died of a fever at age thirty-two. He had never lost a battle.

Alexander founded cities along his route, many named Alexandria, and settled Greek soldiers in them. He married a Persian princess and encouraged his officers to do the same. Was he a visionary uniting peoples or a conqueror who burned Persepolis and killed those who crossed him? The sources say both. How you judge him depends on whether you stand with the Greeks who followed him or the peoples he conquered.

words.d: a kingdom north of Greece whose kings Philip and Alexander conquered the Greek cities and Persia
king of Macedon who conquered the Persian Empire between 334 and 323 BCE
the battle in 331 BCE where Alexander defeated the Persian king Darius III

look.title: Alexander's Campaign
look.prompt: How many years did Alexander spend campaigning in Asia? What problems might an empire face if it was won that fast by one man?

check.q: Who prepared the way for Alexander's conquests by building Macedon's army and controlling Greece?
check.why: Philip II built the professional Macedonian army and defeated the Greek cities in 338 BCE.

check.q: Why did Alexander turn back from India?
choices: His army refused to march farther
He was defeated by the Persians
He ran out of cities to name Alexandria
check.why: After eight years of fighting, his exhausted soldiers would not go on, so he turned around.

check.q: Why might Greeks and Persians remember Alexander differently?
choices: One side saw a hero spreading Greek ways; the other saw a conqueror who burned their capital
check.why: The lesson says judgment depends on whether you stand with those who followed him or those he conquered.

lessons.title: The Hellenistic World
lessons.mainIdea: After Alexander, Greek language and learning blended with Egyptian, Persian and other cultures across a wide Hellenistic world.
reading: Alexander left no clear heir, and his generals fought over his empire for decades. It broke into several kingdoms: Egypt under the family of Ptolemy, much of Asia under the Seleucids, and Macedon itself. Historians call the next three centuries the *Hellenistic* age, from Hellas, the Greek name for Greece. It means Greek-like, because Greek culture spread far beyond Greece and mixed with local ways.

The greatest Hellenistic city was *Alexandria* in Egypt. Its harbor was marked by a lighthouse so tall it was counted among the seven wonders of the world. Its kings built the Museum, a research center, and the famous Library, which aimed to collect every book in the world. Greeks, Egyptians and Jews lived side by side, and the Hebrew scriptures were translated into Greek there.

Scholars in Alexandria and other cities made remarkable discoveries. *Euclid* organized geometry into a system of proofs that students studied for two thousand years. Eratosthenes measured the size of the Earth by comparing shadows in two cities, and came close to the real number. *Archimedes* of Syracuse worked out the law of the lever and the principle of floating bodies. Doctors in Alexandria dissected human bodies and described the nerves.

The Hellenistic world was not simply Greece made bigger. A Greek-speaking merchant in Egypt might pray to a god who was half Greek Zeus and half Egyptian Osiris. Buddhist statues in what is now Pakistan were carved in a Greek style. Greek became the shared language of trade and learning across the eastern Mediterranean, which is why, centuries later, the New Testament was written in Greek.

words.d: the age after Alexander, about 323 to 30 BCE, when Greek culture spread and mixed with others
the Greek-founded city in Egypt famous for its lighthouse, Museum and Library
mathematician in Alexandria who organized geometry into proofs
Greek scientist of Syracuse who explained levers and floating bodies

look.title: Measuring the Earth with Shadows
look.text: Eratosthenes learned that at noon on the longest day, the sun shone straight down a well in Syene, far to the south, casting no shadow. On the same day in Alexandria, a vertical post cast a short shadow at a small angle. He knew the distance between the cities. From the angle and the distance, he calculated the distance around the whole Earth.
look.prompt: What did Eratosthenes have to assume about the shape of the Earth and about the sun's rays for this to work?

check.q: What does the word Hellenistic mean?
choices: Greek-like, a spread and mixing of Greek culture
check.why: It comes from Hellas, Greece, and describes the age when Greek culture spread and mixed with local cultures.

check.q: Which discovery came from the Hellenistic age?
choices: Eratosthenes' measurement of the size of the Earth
check.why: Eratosthenes worked in Alexandria after Alexander. The other choices belong to earlier Greek history.

check.q: What shows that Hellenistic culture was a blend, not just Greek?
choices: Only Greeks could live in Alexandria
Buddhist statues in Greek style and gods that were half Greek, half Egyptian
check.why: The lesson gives these as examples of Greek and local cultures mixing.

lessons.title: Greek Ideas in Our World
lessons.mainIdea: American government, science and everyday English still carry ideas and words that began in ancient Greece.
reading: When the writers of the United States Constitution met in 1787, they had read about Athens. They admired the idea that citizens should govern themselves, but they also feared the Athenian crowd that had executed Socrates and voted for reckless wars. So they chose a *republic* with elected representatives instead of direct democracy. Still, whenever a town holds a meeting where every resident can speak and vote, it is doing what Athenians did on the Pnyx.

Other Greek ideas run through our system. Aristotle wrote that a good constitution mixes rule by one, by a few and by many, and that laws should be above rulers. The jury of ordinary citizens, the idea of a written constitution and the practice of debating in public all have Greek roots. In Illinois, a defendant in a serious case is judged by twelve citizens; an Athenian was judged by hundreds, but the principle is the same.

The Greek habit of asking why, and looking for natural causes, became science. Hippocrates' method of observing patients, Aristotle's classification of living things and Euclid's proofs are still taught. When a doctor takes a medical history, when a biologist sorts species or when a geometry class proves that angles in a triangle add up to a straight line, they are using Greek tools.

Finally, listen to the words. Democracy, politics, philosophy, theater, athlete, marathon, mathematics, biology, physics, geography, history, alphabet, school. All are Greek. About one in ten English words comes from Greek, and in science and medicine the share is far higher. Every time you say telephone or photograph, you are speaking a little Greek.

words.d: a government in which citizens elect representatives to make laws
a system in which citizens vote on laws themselves instead of through representatives
the basic plan and rules for a government, often written down

look.title: Madison on Athens
look.text: In every Athenian assembly, whatever the character of the citizens composing it, the assembly would still have been a mob, had every Athenian citizen been a Socrates.
look.cite: James Madison, Federalist Paper Number 55, 1788 (adapted, key phrase quoted)
look.prompt: Madison praised Athens's citizens but distrusted a large crowd voting directly. What does he think goes wrong in a crowd? Do you agree?

check.q: Why did the writers of the U.S. Constitution choose a republic rather than direct democracy?
choices: They admired self-government but feared the mistakes of a large crowd voting directly
They had never heard of Athens
Greek writings had all been lost
check.why: They took the idea of citizen rule from Athens but chose elected representatives to avoid the dangers they saw in Athens.

check.q: Which modern practice most directly echoes Athenian juries?
choices: Trial by a jury of ordinary citizens
check.why: Athenians judged cases with large citizen juries; an Illinois jury of twelve follows the same principle.

check.q: Roughly what share of English words comes from Greek?
check.why: About one in ten English words is Greek in origin, and in science and medicine the share is much higher.

review.q: How did the geography of Greece shape its politics?
choices: Rich flat farmland led to one large kingdom
Mountains and coasts produced many separate city-states
Deserts forced everyone to live in one city
Rivers united the Greeks under one ruler
review.why: Mountains and the sea cut communities off from each other, so each became its own polis.

review.q: Which reformer created ten tribes and the Council of Five Hundred in 508 BCE?
review.why: Cleisthenes reorganized Athens into tribes and set up the council that prepared business for the assembly.

review.q: Which group in Athens could serve in the army and had to pay taxes but could not vote?
review.why: Metics were free foreigners living in Athens with duties but no political rights.

review.q: Which battle was won mainly by the Athenian navy?
review.why: At Salamis in 480 BCE the Greek fleet destroyed the Persian ships in a narrow strait.

choices: The hill where the Assembly met
A marble temple to Athena on the Acropolis
review.why: The Parthenon was the temple to Athena built between 447 and 432 BCE on the Acropolis.

review.q: Which thinker is known for asking questions and was executed by Athens in 399 BCE?
review.why: Socrates taught by questioning and was sentenced to death by an Athenian jury.

review.q: What made the Hellenistic age different from the earlier Greek world?
choices: Greek culture spread widely and mixed with other cultures
review.why: After Alexander, Greek language and learning blended with Egyptian, Persian and other cultures.

review.q: Which of these is an example of a Greek idea in the United States today?
choices: Trial by a jury of citizens
A council of elders chosen by birth
Boys leaving home at seven for barracks
review.why: Citizen juries began in Athens; the other choices describe Sparta.
